newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals again for campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals again for campaign finance reform.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday pressed his appeal for campaign finance reform and asked broadcasters to give free air time to candidates.

"We have to use the present intense interest in this as well as the controversy over all the fund-raising in the last election and all the publicity on it as a spur to action," Clinton said in a speech to a group dedicated to obtaining free TV time for political candidates as a means of reducing the impact of money on U.S. election campaigns.
"We cannot let it become what it is in danger of becoming, which is an excuse for inaction," he said.

Although he made no mention of a campaign financing probe about to get underway in the Senate, Democrat Clinton seemed to be referring to a decision by Senate Republican leaders not to examine campaign financing loopholes such as a lack of limits on cash given to parties rather than to candidates.

He backs a reform bill that would would ban so-called "soft money" donations -- cash given to the parties for general political purposes and not earmarked for particular candidates. Many see that as a prime source of abuse.

"Do not let the controversy become an excuse to do nothing and to wallow around in it," the president said. "Use it as a spur to change the system because until you change the system, you will have controversies over the amount, the sheer amount of money that is raised in these elections."
The reform bill would also reward candidates who agree to voluntary spending limits with up to 30 minutes of free air time each election on the station or stations of their choice.
Clinton proposed linking free air time for candidates to the advent of high-definition digital television.
"I believe broadcasters who receive digital licenses should provide free air time for candidates," he said. "Free air time for candidates can help free our democracy from the grip of big money."

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt endorsed the proposal, saying the FCC would move ahead with efforts to develop some kind of plan for free air time in exchange for digital-TV licenses.
"I hear the call and I agree with it," Hundt told the same audience after the president's speech.
While seeking reform, Clinton continues to drum up money for fellow Democrats and attended two fund-raisers on Tuesday night that aimed to bring in more than $600,000.

The first, a reception for North Dakota Sen. Byron Dorgan who is up for re-election in 1998, aimed to net as much as $150,000, while the second, a dinner for 40 people, sought to raise $575,000 for the Democratic National Committee.

Clinton's focus on campaign finance reform came as two new polls showed some erosion of his popularity for the first time since he was re-elected, because of concern about fund-raising tactics by the White House and the Democratic Party.

Seventy-two percent of those polled by ABC called reports of Clinton hosting donors at the White House and inviting them to spend the night "inappropriate." Some 59 percent said Clinton did not do anything unlawful, however.
Sixty-two percent said they found Vice President Al Gore's use of his White House office to call donors inappropriate, but 56 percent did not think what he did was illegal.
In a CBS poll, 74 percent said they believed many public officials made or changed policies as a direct result of campaign contributions.
Clinton's approval rating was at 55 percent in the ABC poll, down from 60 percent in January, and at 56 percent in the CBS poll, down from 63 percent two months ago.

"Given the history of the president's approval ratings over the past four years, to be at 55 or 56 percent is not exactly unwelcome news," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters when he was asked about the surveys.
